newsitem.title: USA: USDA tightens rules to keep spinal cord out of meat.
newsitem.headline: USDA tightens rules to keep spinal cord out of meat.

text.p: The Agriculture Department on Friday responded to consumer concern by ordering U.S. meat inspectors to make sure that high-speed machines do not leave any fragments of spinal cord embedded in meat sold to consumers.

In a directive issued to inspectors around the country, the agency alerted them to watch so that high-tech equipment that strips meat from bone does not accidentally add spinal column or marrow to the meat.

"We did see there was some spinal cord in these advanced meat recovery systems," a spokeswoman for the Agriculture Department said. "If there is any suspicion of any spinal cord in the meat, the inspector can take a sample and send it to the laboratory for analysis."

In recent months, consumer groups have urged the Agriculture Department to stop beef companies from processing spinal cord because of a risk that the so-called "mad cow" disease might enter the nation's food supply.
The spinal cord and brain are among the most infectious parts of an animal with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), the disease that broke out in Britain last year.
There have been no cases of BSE in the United States.

The advanced meat recovery systems used by modern slaughter houses produce 300 million to 400 million pounds (136 to 181 kg) of ground meat products annually, which are combined with ground beef, sausages and hot dogs, according to consumer groups.
"There should be no spinal cord in the final product," the Agriculture Department spokeswoman said.
Agriculture Department scientists have developed a method to test samples of ground meat to determine what is muscle meat or spinal cord tissue, she said.
